summary:
CRATER is a mobile-friendly web card game that trains players aged 7–12 to think like the commander of a small Mars outpost. Over 8 sols (Mars days), the player leads a four-person crew (two engineers, a medic, and a botanist) and keeps four meters healthy: Life Support, Radiation Shielding, Power, and Food. Each sol has three cycles (morning, afternoon, night). In every cycle the player is dealt three cards and must pick exactly one, and every card has a cost, so there is never a free choice. A daily summary recaps the decisions made and what they caused.
CRATER addresses the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge by turning real mission constraints (limited resources, delayed effects, and Earth–Mars communication delay) into a short, replayable lesson that needs no download or account. Mission Control guide Noe explains the consequences of each decision and shares NASA-based facts with sources.
details:
WHAT IT DOES?

CRATER is a playable Mars-outpost game for kids aged 7–12. The player is the commander of CRATER Outpost and must keep the crew alive for eight sols. A guide from Mission Control, Noe, introduces the mission, reacts to the player's choices, and writes the ending.

HOW IT WORKS?

Each sol has four phases: Morning (operations), Afternoon (research and exploration), Evening (construction and upgrades), and Night (food and water rations for each crew member). At each card offer the player picks one of three cards or skips, which costs a penalty. Every card changes the four meters (Life Support, Shielding, Power, Food); some effects arrive in a later sol. All meters start at 80/100, and the mission fails if any meter reaches 40 or below, or if the whole crew becomes unwell. Hazards such as dust storms, solar-particle events, airlock leaks, and water or plant-system failures damage the outpost and offer three repair cards. There are five endings: four failures (one for each meter) and one mission-complete ending, each told by Noe, followed by a report with the sol reached, final meter values, and cards played. The player can then restart.

REAL NASA DATA!

The game uses an 80-card catalog (Operations 20, Repair 20, Research 10, Exploration 10, Construction 10, Upgrade 10). Every card carries a fact and source metadata; when a card is played, Noe's message shows its dataset and a link to the NASA source. Sources include ISS life support (ECLSS), OSDR Veggie studies OSD-267 and OSD-269, Curiosity RAD, Curiosity REMS, Perseverance MEDA and MOXIE, InSight, Artemis I MARE radiation measurements, Kilopower, and more. The solar-particle event uses a historical NASA CCMC DONKI record (11 May 2024) mapped to a simulated mission phase. It is not live monitoring, a Mars forecast, or a reading from the outpost; meter effects and hazard timing are game rules, not real predictions.

WHY IT MATTERS?

Kids learn that space missions are about trade-offs, that today's decisions affect tomorrow, and that real NASA missions solved the same problems (dust on solar panels, radiation, water, food). A mission takes minutes, so it fits a classroom or home.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE?

The "no free choice" rule, delayed consequences, hazards that interrupt the plan, rations given to individual crew members, honest feedback from Noe, and real NASA stories shown on every card instead of a separate quiz. All character art, the outpost scene, and the logo are original.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED!

Age-appropriate tone (the crew stays safe in every ending), simple English, being clear about what is real data and what is simulation, source links on every card, and audio that starts only after the first user interaction.

TOOLS

React 19, TypeScript, Phaser 4, Vite 7, Tailwind CSS 4, and Vitest.
